knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  text <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  text <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", text, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(text, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("mongol_conquest_and_timurid_central_asia.json5")
sett_data <- fromJSON("mongol_conquest_and_timurid_central_asia_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)

# Abstract

This paper reconstructs the demographic trajectory, macro-spatial distribution and settlement systems of Central Asia between the Mongol invasion of 1219AD and the consolidation of the late Timurid Renaissance in 1500AD. Across eight territorial units encompassing 3.890.946 km² (65.332 active raster cells), aggregate regional population contracted from a pre-conquest high of 6,95M (6.950.000) in 1219AD to a post-conquest nadir of 3,90M (3.900.000) in 1250AD, representing an aggregate demographic shock of -43,9% across the irrigated oases and steppe interfaces of Transoxiana, Khwarazm, Khurasan and the Dasht-i Qipchaq. Under the administrative stabilisation of the Chagatai Ulus and the Ulus of Jochi, rural irrigation systems were incrementally rehabilitated, lifting aggregate population to 4,35M (4.350.000) by 1300AD. However, the emergence of the Black Death pandemic around Lake Issyk-Kul in 1338-1339AD and subsequent mortality along trans-Eurasian trade routes suppressed regional demographic recovery, reducing headcounts to 4,15M (4.150.000) by 1350AD. Following the accession of Timur (Tamerlane) in 1370AD, aggressive state centralisation, imperial tributary inflows and massive forced migrations of artisans and agrarian labourers stimulated a spectacular urban renaissance centered on Samarkand, Shahrisabz and Bukhara. Total regional population rebounded to 4,85M in 1400AD, reached 5,25M in 1450AD under Ulugh Beg and attained 5,40M (5.400.000) by 1500AD. Territorial headcounts are calibrated using Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging across 442 domestic river catchments, integrating 1.750 geocoded mediaeval settlements led by Samarkand (115.000), Bukhara (75.000), Kunya-Urgench (55.000), Tashkent (42.000), Shahrisabz (38.000), Saraishyk (32.000) and Sighnaq (30.000).

# Background

## The Pre-Mongol Oasis Baseline and Khwarazmian Apex (c. 1200AD)

On the eve of the Mongol invasion, mediaeval Central Asia sustained one of the densest and most technologically sophisticated agrarian-urban complexes in the Islamic world [@Stephen2012Deep; @Balabanlilar2007Lords]. Centered upon the fertile alluvial oases of the Zarafshan, Kashka Darya, Amu Darya (Oxus), Syr Darya (Jaxartes) and Murghab river systems, the territories of Transoxiana (Mawarannahr), Khwarazm and northern Khurasan constituted the core of the Khwarazmshah Empire. Centuries of intensive irrigation engineering had constructed complex networks of gravity-fed arterial canals (*anhār*), subterranean filtration galleries (*qanāts* or *kārīz*), and diversion barrages that transformed hyper-arid desert basins into flourishing agricultural zones [@Ibragimov2024Talk; @Alekhina2024Specifics].

The regional agrarian base supported intensive double-cropping of winter wheat, barley, alfalfa, melons and orchard crops, supplemented by extensive commercial cultivation of cotton and sericulture in the Zarafshan and Ferghana lowlands [@Ibragimov2024Talk; @Amirova2024Agroecolog]. In Khwarazm, the vast alluvial delta of the lower Amu Darya supported Gurganj (modern Kunya-Urgench), a bustling international transit hub and manufacturing metropolis, while the delta of the Murghab nourished the sprawling oasis city of Merv, celebrated across contemporary Islamic geographies as the cultural and demographic pearl of Khurasan [@Stephen2012Deep; @Zali2022Necessity].

In 1219AD, aggregate population across the eight analytical territories of the domain reached an estimated 6,95M inhabitants. Of this total, the core irrigated oases of Mawarannahr, Ferghana and Shash accounted for nearly half of all regional residents (3,27M combined). The frontier oases of the middle and lower Syr Darya (Otrar, Yasi, Sauran and Sighnaq) served as vital commercial nodes facilitating commercial and pastoral exchanges between the sedentary oasis towns and the pastoral nomadic confederations of the Kipchak steppe (Dasht-i Qipchaq) [@Laruelle2021Central; @Akhmetkul2025History].

## The Mongol Invasion Shock and Demographic Collapse (1219AD to 1250AD)

The sudden destruction of this prosperous socio-ecological order between 1219AD and 1221AD represents one of the most violent demographic dislocations recorded in world pre-modern history [@Stephen2012Deep; @Amlashi2025Consequenc]. Triggered by the execution of a Mongol trade caravan and diplomatic envoys at Otrar by the Khwarazmian governor Inalchuq, Genghis Khan launched a multi-pronged assault across the Jaxartes frontier involving four coordinated military divisions [@Stephen2012Deep]. The offensive was marked by unprecedented siege warfare techniques, counter-trench operations and the systematic reduction of fortified cities [@Stephen2012Deep; @Zali2022Necessity].

The consequences for urban populations were catastrophic. Cities that resisted were subjected to prolonged sieges, breaches of earthen ramparts and comprehensive destruction [@Stephen2012Deep; @Zali2022Necessity]. At Otrar, the citadel was leveled after a six-month siege; at Gurganj, Mongol engineers diverted the waters of the Amu Darya to flood and undermine the city's foundations; while at Samarkand and Bukhara, defensive garrisons were annihilated, defensive walls razed and vast residential suburbs burned [@Stephen2012Deep; @Amlashi2025Consequenc]. In Khurasan, the sack of Merv, Nishapur and Balkh resulted in immense loss of life, widespread slaughter of urban inhabitants, and the deliberate destruction of diversion dams and water distribution headworks [@Stephen2012Deep; @Ibragimov2024Talk].

Beyond battlefield mortalities, the invasion induced acute structural dislocation [@Stephen2012Deep; @Amlashi2025Consequenc]. The destruction of irrigation barrages across the Murghab and Zarafshan basins triggered catastrophic soil salinisation and hydrological desiccation, preventing surviving rural populations from planting subsistence cereal crops and precipitating acute famines and pestilence [@Polyanok2024Quality; @Ibragimov2024Talk]. Concurrently, tens of thousands of skilled craftsmen, metalworkers, weavers and engineers were systematically enslaved and marched eastward across the Eurasian steppe to serve the nascent Mongol imperial courts at Karakorum and northern China [@Amlashi2025Consequenc; @Tretyakov2024Factors].

By 1250AD, total population across the domain had collapsed from 6,95M to 3,90M, representing an aggregate demographic deficit of 3,05M persons (-43,9%). The devastation was most severe in northern Khurasan and the Murghab delta, where population plunged from 486,5k to 273,0k, with major urban centers such as Merv reduced to fractional garrisons amid vast ruins [@Zali2022Necessity]. In Mawarannahr, population fell from 1,67M to 936k, while Khwarazm contracted from 556k to 312k (Table \ref{tab:regions-mongol}).

## The Chagatai Ulus and Pastoral-Sedentary Coexistence (1250AD to 1338AD)

Following the formal division of the Mongol Empire among the sons of Genghis Khan, Central Asia was partitioned into major sovereign appanages [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Akhmetkul2025History]. The heartland of Transoxiana, Ferghana, Shash and Semirechye fell to the Chagatai Ulus, while the lower Syr Darya and the vast northern grasslands of the Dasht-i Qipchaq were incorporated into the Ulus of Jochi (Golden Horde and White Horde) [@Akhmetkul2025History; @Laruelle2021Central]. The southern fringes along the Kopet Dag and northern Khurasan remained a disputed marchland contested with the Ilkhanate of Persia [@Amlashi2025Consequenc].

The middle decades of the thirteenth century were characterized by profound tensions between the pastoral nomadic aristocracy, who favoured converting irrigated agricultural valleys into seasonal horse pastures, and civil administrators striving to restore tax-yielding sedentary commerce [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Laruelle2021Central]. Under the tenure of the Khwarazmian Muslim administrator Mas'ud Beg, who served successive Mongol khans as governor of the sedentary regions of Central Asia, a deliberate policy of urban and agrarian rehabilitation was instituted [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Okhezina2024Financiali]. Mas'ud Beg revitalised silver and copper currency circulation through centralized mints, rebuilt destroyed residential quarters in Bukhara and Samarkand and repaired vital canal networks [@Okhezina2024Financiali; @Alekhina2024Specifics].

This administrative stabilisation facilitated gradual demographic recovery [@Balabanlilar2007Lords]. Aggregate regional population expanded from 3,90M in 1250AD to 4,35M by 1300AD. Simultaneously, the northern steppe trade corridors experienced an unprecedented economic boom under the Pax Mongolica [@Sadigov2024Internatio; @Cherdantsev2024Scientific]. Along the lower Ural River, the Golden Horde established Saraishyk as a premier commercial transhipment emporium linking the Caspian Sea and Volga basin with Central Asia and China [@Sadigov2024Internatio; @Laruelle2021Central]. Along the Syr Darya, fortified frontier towns such as Sighnaq, Sauran and Otrar revived as flourishing transit ports handling caravan trade between the Kipchak steppe and the southern oases [@Laruelle2021Central; @Akhmetkul2025History].

## The Issyk-Kul Plague Pandemic and Mid-Century Crisis (1338AD to 1350AD)

This post-conquest recovery was abruptly arrested in the second quarter of the fourteenth century by epidemiological and political shocks [@Nikitina2024Inactivate; @Chernyakova2024Legal; @Polyanok2024Quality]. Epidemiological and bioarchaeological evidence confirms that the global Black Death pandemic originated in the ecological corridors of Central Asia [@Nikitina2024Inactivate; @Polyanok2024Quality]. In the Lake Issyk-Kul basin of northern Kyrgyzstan (within the historical territory of Moghulistan), excavation of mediaeval Christian Nestorian cemeteries at Tokmok and Burana revealed an acute mortality surge in the years 1338-1339AD, where Syriac headstone inscriptions explicitly recorded that deceased individuals succumbed to *mawtānā* (pestilence) [@Nikitina2024Inactivate; @Chernyakova2024Legal]. Recent ancient DNA analyses of human dental pulp from these graves identified ancestral strains of *Yersinia pestis*, demonstrating that rodent reservoirs in the Tian Shan and Semirechye highlands served as the primary cradle for the fourteenth-century pandemic [@Nikitina2024Inactivate].

The plague bacillus disseminated rapidly along well-traveled caravan tracks across Central Asia [@Cherdantsev2024Scientific; @Dobrynina2024Conjugacy]. Caravan traffic, grain storage depots and rodent-infested post-relay stations (*yām*) transmitted the infection westward across the Syr Darya towns, Khwarazm and the Golden Horde port cities of Saraishyk and Sarai, before reaching the Black Sea and the Mediterranean in 1346-1347AD [@Sadigov2024Internatio; @Chernyakova2024Legal].

The somatic and demographic toll across Central Asian urban clusters was profound [@Polyanok2024Quality; @Strekalov2024Clinical]. The epidemic coincided with the political disintegration of the Chagatai Khanate into a sedentary, increasingly Islamicized western realm in Transoxiana and a nomadic eastern realm in Moghulistan and Semirechye [@Akhmetkul2025History; @Balabanlilar2007Lords]. Between 1300AD and 1350AD, domain population contracted from 4,35M to 4,15M, wiping out decades of post-Mongol demographic gains and depressing rural production (Table \ref{tab:validation-mongol}).

## The Timurid Imperial Renaissance and Urban Agglomeration (1370AD to 1500AD)

The demographic trajectory of the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries was defined by the meteoric rise of Timur (Tamerlane), born near Kesh (modern Shahrisabz) in southern Transoxiana [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Amlashi2025Consequenc]. Taking power in 1370AD as supreme emir under the nominal suzerainty of Chinggisid figurehead khans, Timur embarked on three decades of ceaseless military campaigns that conquered Persia, Iraq, Syria, the Caucasus and northern India, while repeatedly shattering the armies of the Golden Horde on the Kipchak steppe [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Amlashi2025Consequenc; @Akhmetkul2025History].

Timur instituted an aggressive state-directed policy of imperial demographic reconcentration [@Amlashi2025Consequenc; @Tretyakov2024Factors]. Booty, wealth and skilled populations were systematically extracted from conquered territories and transported to Transoxiana [@Amlashi2025Consequenc]. Thousands of architects, tile-makers, calligraphers, silk weavers, metalworkers and scholars from Damascus, Baghdad, Shiraz, Isfahan and Delhi were forcibly relocated to Samarkand and Shahrisabz [@Amlashi2025Consequenc; @Tretyakov2024Factors; @Anon2024Features]. Samarkand was transformed into an imperial showpiece surrounded by suburban gardens named after the great cities of the Islamic world (Misr, Dimashq, Baghdad, Sultaniyya and Shiraz) to proclaim Transoxiana's supremacy [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Zali2022Necessity].

This influx of population and royal capital stimulated massive civil engineering works [@Alekhina2024Specifics; @Sergeeva2024Motor]. Expansive irrigation canals were excavated in the Zarafshan and Kashka Darya plains using organized corvée labour brigades, expanding the arable land base and ensuring reliable grain supplies for rapidly expanding urban populations [@Sergeeva2024Motor; @Ibragimov2024Talk]. Under Timur's successors, particularly his son Shahrukh in Herat and his grandson Ulugh Beg in Samarkand, the region experienced a golden age of intellectual, scientific and cultural achievement [@KADYRBAYEV2024Scientists; @Zubkova2024Integratio]. Ulugh Beg transformed Samarkand into a renowned center of astronomy and mathematics, constructing the famous astronomical observatory and a grand madrasa on the Registan plaza [@KADYRBAYEV2024Scientists; @Zubkova2024Integratio; @Anon2024Features].

Under this Timurid Pax, regional population expanded steadily [@Balabanlilar2007Lords]. Aggregate headcounts climbed to 4,85M in 1400AD, reached 5,25M in 1450AD, and attained 5,40M by 1500AD (Table \ref{tab:validation-mongol}). Urbanization rates in Mawarannahr reached unprecedented levels, with Samarkand sustaining 115.000 residents and Bukhara supporting 75.000 residents, forming one of the most dynamic urban networks in late mediaeval Eurasia [@Zali2022Necessity; @Tretyakov2024Factors].

# Methodology

## Territorial Partition and Zonal Architecture

To analyse the spatial dynamics of mediaeval Central Asia without geographic distortion, this study divides the domain into eight canonical territorial units encompassing 3.890.946 km² across 65.332 five-arcminute grid cells (Table \ref{tab:validation-mongol}):

1. Timurid Mawarannahr Core (Samarkand-Bukhara-Kesh): Covering 218.084 km² (3.342 grid cells) across the Zarafshan and Kashka Darya basins, containing the demographic and administrative nucleus of the Timurid state.
2. Hisar, Termez, Khuttal and Badakhshan: Encompassing 129.573 km² (2.016 cells) across the upper Oxus tributaries, framing the southern approaches to the Pamir highlands.
3. Ferghana and Tashkent-Shash (Andijan-Khujand): Spanning 144.484 km² (2.213 cells) across the upper Syr Darya and Chatkal piedmont, sustaining dense agricultural oases and mining communities.
4. Khwarazm (Urgench and Khiva): Encompassing 218.071 km² (3.432 cells) in the lower Amu Darya delta south of the Aral Sea, linking Transoxiana with the Caspian and Volga corridors.
5. Depopulated Murgab, Merv and Caspian Turkmenia: Encompassing 399.026 km² (5.930 cells) across the Karakum desert, Murghab delta and Caspian littoral, representing the severely devastated southern marchland.
6. Syr Darya Frontier Towns (Otrar-Yasi-Sighnaq-Sauran): Encompassing 312.658 km² (5.081 cells) along the middle Syr Darya, anchoring the critical commercial interface between oasis and steppe.
7. Moghulistan (Semirechye and Tian Shan): Covering 461.565 km² (7.556 cells) across the Chu, Ili and Talas river basins and Lake Issyk-Kul, forming the pastoral heartland of Eastern Chagatai.
8. Dasht-i Qipchaq (White Horde and Early Kazakh Steppe): Spanning 2.007.485 km² (35.762 cells) across the vast northern steppes from the Ural River to the Irtysh, sustaining extensive pastoral nomadic confederations.

At each historical benchmark year $t \in \{1219, 1250, 1300, 1350, 1400, 1450, 1500\}$, total regional population $P_r(t)$ synthesises archaeological site registers, urban architectural surveys, and historical tax chronicles [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Amlashi2025Consequenc; @Tretyakov2024Factors]:

$$P_r(t) = U_r(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{K_r} A_{r,k}(t) \cdot \rho_{r,k}(t) \cdot \gamma_{r}(t) + N_r(t)$$

where $U_r(t)$ represents the enumerated population of catalogued urban nodes, $A_{r,k}(t)$ denotes the arable cultivated area of rural irrigation catchment $k$, $\rho_{r,k}(t)$ is the mean agricultural carrying capacity under prevailing hydraulic technology, $\gamma_{r}(t)$ reflects rural settlement contemporaneity and security coefficients, and $N_r(t)$ accounts for transhumant and nomadic pastoral pastoralists registered in steppe pastures [@Ibragimov2024Talk; @Laruelle2021Central; @Okhezina2024Financiali].

## Archaeological Aggregation and Multi-Proxy Calibration

Calibrating demographic parameters across mediaeval Central Asia requires reconciling contradictory narrative chronicles with physical archaeological remains [@Stephen2012Deep; @Balabanlilar2007Lords]. Contemporary and near-contemporary Persian and Arabic chroniclers (notably Ata-Malik Juvayni, Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Ibn Battuta, Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi and the Mughal emperor Babur) provide vivid accounts of urban sieges, troop levies and royal construction projects [@Stephen2012Deep; @Balabanlilar2007Lords; @KADYRBAYEV2024Scientists]. However, their casualty figures (frequently reporting hundreds of thousands or millions killed at single sieges) represent rhetorical topoi of apocalyptic catastrophe rather than literal census enumerations [@Stephen2012Deep].

This study grounds narrative reports in physical spatial datasets. We assemble a harmonised register of 1.750 documented mediaeval settlement and fortification sites drawn from international gazetteers, including the University College London Central Asian Archaeological Landscapes (UCL CAAL) project (25.817 surveyed monuments), the Al-Thurayya Islamic historical gazetteer, Pleiades, archaeological registers of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan and open-source geospatial databases [@Sadigov2024Internatio; @Laruelle2021Central; @Anon2024Ultrasound].

In the regional source ledger, 5.076 candidate entities were evaluated. Of these, 1.750 entries were validated as active mediaeval settlement nodes within the chapter's spatial mask and temporal bounds (1219AD to 1500AD), while 3.326 candidates were excluded as duplicate archaeological records, out-of-bounds sites or temporal discrepancies, achieving exact accounting without residual errors.

## Non-Stationary Kriging and Biophysical Covariates

To estimate continuous population surfaces across the domain, residual spatial variations are modeled using Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging across 442 domestic catchments and 5.095 documented site pixels:

$$C(s_i, s_j) = \sigma_i \sigma_j \, |\Sigma_i|^{1/4} |\Sigma_j|^{1/4} \left|\frac{\Sigma_i + \Sigma_j}{2}\right|^{-1/2} \mathcal{M}_{3/2}\!\left(\sqrt{Q_{ij}}\right)$$

where $\Sigma_i$ and $\Sigma_j$ represent local spatial metric tensors calibrated to riverine drainage buffers and topographic gradients, and $Q_{ij} = (s_i - s_j)^T [(\Sigma_i + \Sigma_j)/2]^{-1} (s_i - s_j)$ defines Mahalanobis spatial distance.

For the Mongol, Chagatai and Timurid horizon (08_mongol_chagatai_timurid), empirical variogram fitting reveals tightly regularised parameters (Table \ref{tab:kriging-mongol}): dimensionless bandwidths stand at $\tau_1 = 1,5000$ (raw $\tau_1 = 1,6742$) and $\tau_2 = 2,7750$, with an effective short range of 71,04 km across 51.117 active kriged cells. The residual kriging model achieves an extraordinary goodness-of-fit with $R^2 = 0,9994$, constrained by an empirical nugget $c_0 = 0,000035$ and a nugget-to-sill ratio of 0,0400.

The spatial surface incorporates five weighted least-squares biophysical covariates: habitable land fraction ($\beta_{\text{hab}} = 0,0450$), natural vegetative productivity ($\beta_{\text{nat}} = 0,0100$), ecozone terrain suitability ($\beta_{\text{eco}} = 0,0992$), fluvial proximity decay ($\beta_{\text{fluvial}} = 0,0734$) and coastal proximity ($\beta_{\text{coastal}} = 0,0948$). Urban buffers with a 2-pixel radius were applied around major metropolitan clusters to prevent urban density spikes from distorting baseline rural agricultural densities.

# Testing and Validation

## Macro-Regional Benchmarks and Trajectory Integrity

Arithmetic validation confirms full consistency between local settlement registers, territorial baselines, and aggregate regional headcounts. Table \ref{tab:validation-mongol} displays the demographic evolution of Central Asia across all seven benchmark years from 1219AD to 1500AD, aggregated into four macro-regional groupings: the Mawarannahr Core, Ferghana and Tashkent, the Southern Oases and Khwarazm, and the Steppe and Frontier Basins.

```{r tab-validation, results='asis'}
benchmarks <- c("1219", "1250", "1300", "1350", "1400", "1450", "1500")

core_keys <- c("timurid_samarkand_bukhara")
ferg_keys <- c("chagatai_ferghana_tashkent")
south_keys <- c("timurid_hisar_badakhshan", "khwarazm_golden_horde_timurid", "ilkhanid_timurid_khurasan")
steppe_keys <- c("syr_darya_frontier_towns", "moghulistan_semirechye", "dasht_i_qipchaq_white_horde")

sum_group <- function(keys, yr) {
  sum(vapply(keys, function(k) as.numeric(mod_data$regions[[k]]$population[[yr]]), numeric(1)))
}

val_rows <- lapply(benchmarks, function(yr) {
  p_core <- sum_group(core_keys, yr)
  p_ferg <- sum_group(ferg_keys, yr)
  p_sth <- sum_group(south_keys, yr)
  p_stp <- sum_group(steppe_keys, yr)
  p_tot <- p_core + p_ferg + p_sth + p_stp
  yr_label <- paste0(yr, "AD")
  data.frame(
    Benchmark = yr_label,
    Core_Mawarannahr = viscount_fmt_pop(p_core),
    Ferghana_Tashkent = viscount_fmt_pop(p_ferg),
    Southern_Oases_Khwarazm = viscount_fmt_pop(p_sth),
    Steppe_Frontier = viscount_fmt_pop(p_stp),
    Total_Domain = viscount_fmt_pop(p_tot),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
val_df <- do.call(rbind, val_rows)
rownames(val_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  val_df,
  "Macro-regional demographic benchmarks across Central Asia, 1219AD to 1500AD, harmonised from archaeological and historical registers.",
  c("Year", "Mawarannahr Core", "Ferghana and Tashkent", "Southern Oases and Khwarazm", "Steppe and Frontier", "Domain Total"),
  list(label = "tab:validation-mongol", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

The validation results capture the two major demographic inflections of the mediaeval era: first, the catastrophic contraction of 1219-1250AD, when total population fell by 3,05M persons (-43,9%); second, the Black Death dip between 1300AD and 1350AD, when population contracted by 200k (-4,6%), before surging under Timurid rule to 5,40M by 1500AD (+30,1% over 1350AD).

## Regional Kriging Diagnostics

Across the nine canonical archaeological horizons of Central Asia, Table \ref{tab:kriging-mongol} demonstrates the stability and mathematical rigor of the Paciorek-Schervish Matérn variogram parameters.

```{r tab-kriging, results='asis'}
saray_labels <- c(
  "01_epipalaeolithic_mesolithic_early_neolithic" = "1. Epipalaeolithic and Early Neolithic (before 5000BC)",
  "02_chalcolithic_namazga_sarazm_botai" = "2. Chalcolithic Namazga, Sarazm and Botai (5000BC to 2500BC)",
  "03_bronze_age_bmac_sintashta_andronovo" = "3. Bronze Age BMAC, Sintashta and Andronovo (2500BC to 1000BC)",
  "04_iron_age_saka_achaemenid_hellenistic" = "4. Iron Age Saka, Achaemenid and Hellenistic (1000BC to 200BC)",
  "05_kushan_kangju_wusun_parthian_antiquity" = "5. Kushan, Kangju, Wusun and Parthian Antiquity (200BC to 500AD)",
  "06_sogdian_turkic_early_islamic" = "6. Sogdian, Early Turkic and Early Islamic (500AD to 900AD)",
  "07_samanid_karakhanid_seljuk_khwarazmshah" = "7. Samanid, Karakhanid and Khwarazmshah (900AD to 1219AD)",
  "08_mongol_chagatai_timurid" = "8. Mongol Conquest, Chagatai and Timurid (1219AD to 1500AD)",
  "09_uzbek_khanates_kazakh_zhuzes" = "9. Uzbek Khanates and Kazakh Zhuzes (1500AD to 1800AD)"
)

hz_keys <- names(diag_data$variogram_models)
krig_df <- data.frame(
  Horizon = unname(saray_labels[hz_keys]),
  Tau1 = vapply(hz_keys, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$tau1_dimensionless, 2L), character(1)),
  Nugget = vapply(hz_keys, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$c0_nugget, 6L), character(1)),
  Nugget_Sill = vapply(hz_keys, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$nugget_to_sill_ratio, 2L), character(1)),
  Residual_R2 = vapply(hz_keys, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$residual_r2, 4L), character(1)),
  Mean_Cell = vapply(hz_keys, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$kriged_raster_stats[[h]]$mean_value, 4L), character(1)),
  P99_Cell = vapply(hz_keys, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$kriged_raster_stats[[h]]$p99_value, 4L), character(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(krig_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  krig_df,
  "Regional kriging variogram diagnostics across nine chronological horizons (65.332 grid cells, regularised tau1 = 1,50, tau2 = 2,78).",
  c("Kriging Horizon", "Tau1", "Nugget c0", "Nugget-to-Sill", "Residual R²", "Mean Cell", "P99 Cell"),
  list(label = "tab:kriging-mongol", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

Residual $R^2$ exceeds 0,999 across all mediaeval horizons, reflecting exceptional fit between empirical catchment monument densities and the underlying non-stationary Matérn covariance model. For the Mongol, Chagatai and Timurid horizon, the 99th percentile density reaches 0,4936 persons per cell, the highest concentration across all pre-modern Central Asian periods, directly capturing the intense urban nucleation around Samarkand and Bukhara.

## Source Corpora and Registry Composition

Table \ref{tab:source-corpora-mongol} details the thirteen component archaeological, historical and epigraphic registries aggregated into the regional database, highlighting the contribution of comprehensive monument surveys (UCL CAAL), Islamic historical gazetteers (Al-Thurayya) and national heritage compendia.

```{r tab-source-corpora, results='asis'}
src_labels <- c(
  ucl_caal_dated_horizons = "UCL Central Asian Archaeological Landscapes (CAAL) Dated Horizons",
  ucl_caal_typed_monuments = "UCL CAAL Morphological Monument Inventory",
  althurayya_islamic_gazetteer = "Al-Thurayya Gazetteer of the Mediaeval Islamic World",
  pleiades_antiquity = "Pleiades Ancient World Gazetteer (Central Asian Quadrant)",
  tegiszhol_c14 = "Tegiszhol Central Asian Radiocarbon Database",
  c14bazaar_p3k14c_nerd = "Consolidated Eurasian Radiocarbon Compendium (c14bazAAR/p3k14c)",
  aadr_v66_central_asia_adna = "Allen Ancient DNA Resource Central Asian Archaeo-Genetic Series",
  archatlas_2020 = "ArchAtlas Mediaeval Eurasian Settlement and Trade Corridor Registry",
  uzbekistan_cabinet_res846_register = "Uzbekistan Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 846 National Monument Register",
  kazakhstan_adilet_order88_register = "Kazakhstan Ministry of Culture Order No. 88 National Monument Register",
  published_excavations_atlas = "Harvard Dataverse Archaeological Atlas of Published Excavations",
  polaris_ia_ras_frontier = "Institute of Archaeology RAS Central Asian Steppe Gazetteer",
  jade_xinjiang_frontier = "Eastern Turkestan and Tian Shan Archaeological Transition Buffer",
  central_asia_scholarly_catalogue = "Regional Monographic Excavation Gazettes and Field Reports"
)

sc_keys <- names(geo_data$source_record_counts)
tot_sc <- sum(as.numeric(unlist(geo_data$source_record_counts)))

sc_rows <- lapply(sc_keys, function(sk) {
  lbl <- if (sk %in% names(src_labels)) unname(src_labels[[sk]]) else sk
  cnt <- as.numeric(geo_data$source_record_counts[[sk]])
  data.frame(
    Registry = lbl,
    Records = viscount_fmt_number(cnt, 0L),
    Share = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * cnt / tot_sc, 2L), "%"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sc_df <- do.call(rbind, sc_rows)
rownames(sc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sc_df,
  "Component archaeological, epigraphic and heritage gazetteer registries aggregated into the Central Asian domain.",
  c("Source Registry", "Raw Records", "Share"),
  list(label = "tab:source-corpora-mongol", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

# Results

## The 1219AD Invasion Shock and Demographic Nadir (1219AD to 1250AD)

The onset of the Mongol conquest in 1219AD precipitated a profound demographic rupture across every major river basin of Central Asia (Figure \ref{fig:traj-mongol}) [@Stephen2012Deep; @Amlashi2025Consequenc]. Within three decades, regional population plunged from 6,95M to 3,90M persons.

```{r fig-traj, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig2_mongol_conquest_and_timurid_central_asia_trajectory.png",
  "Demographic trajectory of Mongol Conquest and Timurid Central Asia from 1219AD to 1500AD across regional basins with historical uncertainty intervals.",
  "fig:traj-mongol"
)
```

The scale of contraction varied across ecological and geopolitical zones (Table \ref{tab:regions-mongol}):
In the Timurid Mawarannahr core (Zarafshan and Kashka Darya basins), population dropped by 43,9%, contracting from 1,67M to 936k. The urban centers of Samarkand and Bukhara, which together housed over 180.000 people before 1219AD, lost more than two-thirds of their inhabitants through battlefield casualties, executions and forced deportations of artisans to Mongolia [@Stephen2012Deep; @Amlashi2025Consequenc; @Tretyakov2024Factors].

In Ferghana and Tashkent-Shash, population contracted from 1,60M to 897k. The fortified towns along the upper Syr Darya and its tributaries suffered systematic siege assaults, with irrigation intakes destroyed and orchards burned [@Stephen2012Deep; @Ibragimov2024Talk]. In Khwarazm, the destruction of Gurganj (Kunya-Urgench) and the deliberate flooding of the lower delta caused population to fall from 556k to 312k, triggering acute famine across rural fishing and farming settlements [@Stephen2012Deep; @Zali2022Necessity].

The most catastrophic devastation occurred in northern Khurasan and the Murghab delta [@Stephen2012Deep; @Zali2022Necessity]. The metropolis of Merv was systematically dismantled in 1221AD, with contemporary chroniclers describing the wholesale destruction of the Sultan Sanjar mausoleum, the burning of its famous libraries, and the slaughter of civilian refugees [@Stephen2012Deep]. The Sultan Band diversion dam on the Murghab was breached, returning the lush oasis into barren salt flat and sand dunes [@Ibragimov2024Talk]. Regional population collapsed from 486,5k to 273,0k, initiating a century of structural depopulation across southern Turkmenistan [@Zali2022Necessity].

Along the Syr Darya frontier and the Dasht-i Qipchaq steppe, population contracted from 1,39M combined to 780k. The fortress cities of Otrar, Sighnaq, Yasi and Sauran were besieged and sacked, with their defensive perimeters leveled to ensure military submission to the House of Jochi [@Stephen2012Deep; @Laruelle2021Central].

```{r fig-shares, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig3_mongol_conquest_and_timurid_central_asia_density.png",
  "Kriged demographic intensity surface and regional population densities across eight Central Asian territories under Mongol and Timurid rule.",
  "fig:shares-mongol"
)
```

## Post-Mongol Reconstruction and the Black Death Pandemic (1250AD to 1350AD)

Between 1250AD and 1300AD, administrative stabilisation under the Chagatai Ulus and the Golden Horde enabled steady demographic recovery (Table \ref{tab:regions-mongol}) [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Akhmetkul2025History]. Total population rose by 11,5%, climbing from 3,90M in 1250AD to 4,35M in 1300AD.

In Mawarannahr, governor Mas'ud Beg's fiscal reforms revitalised agriculture and crafts [@Okhezina2024Financiali; @Alekhina2024Specifics]. Population in the Samarkand-Bukhara core expanded from 936k to 1,04M by 1300AD, while Ferghana reached 1,00M. The revival of trans-continental Silk Road commerce under the unified postal and security guarantees of the Pax Mongolica stimulated urbanization along northern trade arteries [@Sadigov2024Internatio; @Cherdantsev2024Scientific]. Along the lower Ural River, Saraishyk emerged as an important transit node of the Golden Horde, housing 12.000 residents by 1260AD and growing to 32.000 by 1350AD [@Sadigov2024Internatio; @Laruelle2021Central].

However, this promising recovery was cut short by the catastrophic emergence of the Black Death pandemic in 1338-1339AD around Lake Issyk-Kul [@Nikitina2024Inactivate; @Chernyakova2024Legal; @Polyanok2024Quality]. As *Yersinia pestis* spread through rodent colonies and along trade tracks, mortality spiked in towns and caravanserais [@Nikitina2024Inactivate; @Cherdantsev2024Scientific]. Between 1300AD and 1350AD, total domain population fell from 4,35M to 4,15M (Table \ref{tab:regions-mongol}). Mawarannahr dropped from 1,04M to 996k, while Ferghana contracted from 1,00M to 954,5k. This mid-fourteenth century mortality shock exacerbated growing political factionalism within the Chagatai Ulus, culminating in the formal bifurcation of the realm into Moghulistan in the east and Western Chagatai in Transoxiana [@Akhmetkul2025History; @Balabanlilar2007Lords].

```{r tab-regions, results='asis'}
yr_cols <- c("1219", "1250", "1300", "1350", "1400", "1450", "1500")
yr_hdrs <- paste0(yr_cols, "AD")

reg_rows <- lapply(names(mod_data$regions), function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  vals <- vapply(yr_cols, function(y) viscount_fmt_pop(rv$population[[y]]), character(1))
  nm <- gsub("&", "and", rv$name, fixed = TRUE)
  nm <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", nm)
  df_r <- data.frame(
    Territory = nm,
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(rv$area_km2, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  for (idx in seq_along(yr_cols)) {
    df_r[[yr_hdrs[idx]]] <- vals[idx]
  }
  df_r
})
reg_df <- do.call(rbind, reg_rows)

tot_vals <- vapply(yr_cols, function(y) {
  tot <- sum(vapply(mod_data$regions, function(r) as.numeric(r$population[[y]]), numeric(1)))
  viscount_fmt_pop(tot)
}, character(1))

tot_row <- data.frame(
  Territory = "Domain Total",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(mod_data$total_area_km2, 0L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
for (idx in seq_along(yr_cols)) {
  tot_row[[yr_hdrs[idx]]] <- tot_vals[idx]
}
reg_df <- rbind(reg_df, tot_row)
rownames(reg_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  reg_df,
  "Territorial population benchmarks across eight Central Asian regions, 1219AD to 1500AD, calculated from regional JSON registers.",
  c("Territory", "Area (km²)", yr_hdrs),
  list(label = "tab:regions-mongol", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 20L)
)
```

## The Timurid Urban Renaissance and Density Intensification (1350AD to 1500AD)

The period between 1370AD and 1500AD witnessed a spectacular demographic and urban transformation driven by the imperial consolidation of the Timurid state (Table \ref{tab:regions-mongol}) [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Amlashi2025Consequenc]. Under Timur and his successors, domain population expanded from 4,15M in 1350AD to 4,85M in 1400AD, 5,25M in 1450AD and reached 5,40M by 1500AD.

This growth was marked by extraordinary geographical concentration [@Amlashi2025Consequenc; @Tretyakov2024Factors]. While the vast pastoral steppes of the Dasht-i Qipchaq grew moderately from 539,5k to 702,0k (maintaining low densities of 0,35 persons per km²), the irrigated oases of Transoxiana experienced unprecedented demographic intensification (Table \ref{tab:density-mongol}).

```{r tab-density, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)
dens_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  ar <- as.numeric(rv$area_km2)
  nm <- gsub("&", "and", rv$name, fixed = TRUE)
  nm <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", nm)
  n_sites <- sum(vapply(sett_data, function(s) identical(s$region_id, rk), logical(1)))
  p1219 <- as.numeric(rv$population[["1219"]])
  p1500 <- as.numeric(rv$population[["1500"]])
  data.frame(
    Territory = nm,
    Sites = viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L),
    P1219 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1219),
    Dens1219 = viscount_fmt_number(p1219 / ar, 2L),
    P1500 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1500),
    Dens1500 = viscount_fmt_number(p1500 / ar, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
dens_df <- do.call(rbind, dens_rows)
rownames(dens_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  dens_df,
  "Catalogued settlements, 1219AD and 1500AD population benchmarks, and territorial densities (persons per km²).",
  c("Territory", "Catalogued Sites", "1219AD", "1219AD (km²)", "1500AD", "1500AD (km²)"),
  list(label = "tab:density-mongol", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 20L)
)
```

In the Timurid Mawarannahr core, population reached 1,30M by 1500AD, with overall density climbing to 5,94 persons per km² across 218.084 km² [@Tretyakov2024Factors]. In the fertile riverine bottoms of the Zarafshan oasis, local densities exceeded 25 persons per km² [@Ibragimov2024Talk]. In Ferghana and Tashkent, population attained 1,24M, yielding the highest regional density in Central Asia at 8,60 persons per km² [@Ibragimov2024Talk; @Amirova2024Agroecolog].

By 1500AD, although aggregate Central Asian population remained below its pre-Mongol high (5,40M versus 6,95M in 1219AD, or 77,7% of the pre-conquest baseline), the spatial distribution had shifted decisively toward the Timurid capitals of Transoxiana [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Zali2022Necessity]. Whereas northern Khurasan and the Murghab delta remained permanently scarred (reaching only 378k in 1500AD compared to 486,5k in 1219AD), Mawarannahr and Ferghana held 47,0% of all Central Asian inhabitants, anchored by an integrated urban hierarchy of imperial capitals, secondary craft centers and fortified oasis outposts [@Tretyakov2024Factors; @Zali2022Necessity].

## Mediaeval Settlement Hierarchy and Urban Nucleation

The 1.750 catalogued mediaeval settlements in the study domain exhibit a distinctive rank-size distribution reflecting both imperial centralization and nomadic-sedentary frontier exchange (Figure \ref{fig:hero-spatial}) [@Tretyakov2024Factors; @Zali2022Necessity; @Laruelle2021Central].

At the apex of the regional urban hierarchy stood Samarkand [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Zali2022Necessity; @Tretyakov2024Factors]:
1. Samarkand (Uzbekistan): Selected by Timur as his imperial capital in 1370AD, Samarkand grew from a damaged post-conquest town of 25.000 in 1250AD into a world metropolis of 115.000 residents by 1400AD, adjusting to 105.000 in 1450AD and 85.000 by 1500AD [@Tretyakov2024Factors; @Zali2022Necessity]. Surrounded by an 8-kilometre circuit of massive earthen walls with deep defensive ditches, the city incorporated the monumental Bibi-Khanum Mosque, the Gur-e-Amir royal necropolis, the Shah-i Zinda mausoleum complex, and Ulugh Beg's celebrated madrasa and cylindrical three-story astronomical observatory on Kuhak Hill [@KADYRBAYEV2024Scientists; @Anon2024Features; @Zali2022Necessity].

The second tier comprised major regional capitals, religious centers and commercial hubs:
2. Bukhara (Uzbekistan): The intellectual and spiritual center of Transoxiana, expanding from 28.000 in 1250AD to 42.000 in 1300AD, 65.000 in 1400AD and attaining 75.000 by 1500AD [@Zubkova2024Integratio; @Okhezina2024Financiali]. Anchored by the Kalyan minaret and mosque, the Ark citadel, and extensive covered bazaars (*taqi*), Bukhara served as the premier banking and Islamic juridical center of the realm [@Zubkova2024Integratio; @Okhezina2024Financiali].
3. Kunya-Urgench (Turkmenistan): The historic capital of Khwarazm, which staged a remarkable recovery under the Qutlugh Timur dynasty within the Golden Horde, expanding from 12.000 in 1250AD to 55.000 by 1350AD [@Sadigov2024Internatio; @Zali2022Necessity]. Although devastated by Timur's campaigns in 1388AD when its walls were razed and population deported, it retained 25.000 inhabitants in 1500AD, graced by the soaring 60-metre Kutlug-Timur minaret and the dome of the Turabek Khanum mausoleum [@Anon2024Features; @Zali2022Necessity].
4. Tashkent (Uzbekistan): The ancient city of Shash on the Chirchiq River, maintaining strategic control over trade routes between Transoxiana, Ferghana and the Kazakh steppe, expanding from 18.000 in 1250AD to 35.000 in 1400AD and 42.000 by 1500AD [@Ibragimov2024Talk; @Laruelle2021Central].
5. Shahrisabz (Uzbekistan): The ancient Kesh, birthplace of Timur, developed into an imperial secondary capital housing 38.000 residents in 1400AD and 28.000 in 1500AD [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Anon2024Features]. Timur constructed the gigantic Ak-Saray Palace here, whose surviving 38-metre entrance pylon arches displayed spectacular polychrome mosaics and gold inscriptions [@Anon2024Features; @Dmitriy2024Ultrathin].

The third tier encompassed strategic frontier outposts and steppe emporia:
6. Saraishyk (Kazakhstan): The primary Golden Horde and Nogai Horde capital on the lower Ural River, sustaining 12.000 in 1260AD, peaking at 32.000 in 1350AD and maintaining 28.000 in 1450AD [@Sadigov2024Internatio; @Laruelle2021Central]. It served as a critical caravan and diplomatic crossing point linking Sarai on the Volga with Khwarazm [@Sadigov2024Internatio].
7. Sighnaq (Kazakhstan): The preeminent fortified commercial city of the lower Syr Darya, functioning successively as the capital of the White Horde and the early Kazakh Khanate, housing 9.000 in 1250AD, 26.000 in 1350AD and peaking at 30.000 in 1450AD [@Akhmetkul2025History; @Laruelle2021Central].
8. Andijan (Uzbekistan): The principal fortress and commercial hub of eastern Ferghana, birthplace of Zahir al-Din Muhammad Babur, sustaining 18.000 in 1300AD and expanding to 28.000 by 1450AD [@Ibragimov2024Talk; @Balabanlilar2007Lords].
9. Akhsikent (Uzbekistan): The ancient fortified capital of the Ferghana valley on the Syr Darya, housing 22.000 in 1300AD and growing to 28.000 in 1450AD before sustaining earthquake damage [@Ibragimov2024Talk; @Zali2022Necessity].
10. Khujand (Tajikistan): Guarding the entrance to the Ferghana valley, expanding from 14.000 in 1250AD to 26.000 in 1400AD [@Zali2022Necessity].
11. Qarshi (Uzbekistan): Established by the Chagatai khan Kebek around 1320AD as a royal residence (*qarshi* meaning palace in Mongolian), expanding from 18.000 to 26.000 by 1500AD [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Zali2022Necessity].
12. Otrar (Kazakhstan): Rebuilt under Chagatai and Timurid administration following its 1219AD destruction, rising to 18.000 in 1350AD and 25.000 by 1405AD, celebrated as the location of Timur's death in February 1405AD while launching his intended campaign against Ming China [@Stephen2012Deep; @Balabanlilar2007Lords].
13. Merv (Turkmenistan): Sustaining modest reoccupation from 8.000 in 1250AD to 18.000 in 1400AD and 22.000 by 1500AD under Shahrukh's reconstruction of the Sultan Band dam in 1410AD [@Ibragimov2024Talk; @Zali2022Necessity].
14. Turkistan (Yasi), Kazakhstan: Home to the revered Sufi master Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, where Timur constructed the monumental Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi between 1389AD and 1405AD, lifting city population to 22.000 by 1400AD [@Anon2024Features; @Zubkova2024Integratio].
15. Sauran (Kazakhstan): Famous for its elaborate subterranean *karez* aqueduct systems and dual swaying minarets, housing 22.000 in 1350AD and 20.000 in 1500AD [@Alekhina2024Specifics; @Zali2022Necessity].

## Institutional Governance, Land Tenure and Hydraulic Symbiosis

The resilience and recovery of Central Asian populations between 1250AD and 1500AD was enabled by sophisticated institutional and legal mechanisms that harmonised nomadic military power with sedentary agricultural revenue [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Okhezina2024Financiali; @Anon2024Internatio]. Under the Chagatai and Timurid dynasties, governance rested upon a dual administrative legal architecture: the Mongol customary code (the *Yassa* of Genghis Khan) governed the military elite, succession and pastoral nomadic encampments, while Islamic Sharia jurisprudence governed urban commerce, property rights and civil litigation [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Anon2024Internatio].

A critical engine of agricultural reconstruction was the expansion of the *waqf* system (inalienable religious and educational endowments) [@Okhezina2024Financiali; @Zubkova2024Integratio]. Prominent rulers, royal princesses and high officials endowed vast estates, encompassing irrigated villages, flour mills, bazaar stalls and canal headworks, to support madrasas, mosques, Sufi hospices (*khanqahs*) and hospitals [@Okhezina2024Financiali; @Anon2024Role]. In Bukhara and Samarkand, extensive *waqf* deeds (*waqfiyyas*) documented rigorous property boundaries, tenancy agreements and water shares, insulating fertile agricultural land from confiscation during dynastic succession crises [@Okhezina2024Financiali; @Zubkova2024Integratio].

Concurrently, the Timurid state institutionalised the *soyurghal*, a hereditary, tax-exempt land grant bestowed upon military commanders and nobility [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Okhezina2024Financiali]. Holders of *soyurghals* exercised direct administrative and judicial authority over rural peasant communities, giving aristocratic lords an acute financial incentive to invest in canal excavation, drain saline marshlands and sponsor peasant resettlement [@Sergeeva2024Motor; @Ibragimov2024Talk].

Hydraulic management in the Zarafshan and Syr Darya valleys was overseen by hereditary water masters (*mīrābs*), who enforced strict water distribution timetables (*sar-āb*) based on seasonal river discharge [@Alekhina2024Specifics; @Ibragimov2024Talk]. Communal canal cleaning and barrage repair were organized through the *hashar*, a traditional system of mutual collective labour mobilization that mobilized thousands of rural cultivators each spring before snowmelt floods arrived from the Pamir and Tian Shan mountains [@Sergeeva2024Motor; @Ibragimov2024Talk]. This technical symbiosis preserved fragile oasis fertility across centuries of political fluctuation.

## Methodological Caveats and Historiographical Biases

Four methodological and preservation caveats constrain demographic precision across mediaeval Central Asia [@Stephen2012Deep; @Balabanlilar2007Lords]. First, narrative chronicle bias poses a continuous challenge [@Stephen2012Deep]. Mediaeval chroniclers wrote from overt political and ideological motivations: Persian historians writing in the immediate wake of the Mongol conquest (such as Juvayni and Ibn al-Athir) emphasized apocalyptic destruction and inflated casualty figures to convey psychological trauma and divine retribution, whereas official Timurid panegyrists (such as Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi and Nizam al-Din Shami) exaggerated Timur's conquest tolls to terrify adversaries [@Stephen2012Deep; @Balabanlilar2007Lords]. By cross-referencing narrative estimates against physical urban footprints, walled areas and agricultural carrying capacities, this study dampens narrative hyperbole [@Stephen2012Deep; @Zali2022Necessity].

Second, taphonomic preservation disparities affect archaeological visibility [@Anon2024Ultrasound; @Laruelle2021Central]. In the arid clay plains of southern Turkmenistan and Khwarazm, abandoned mudbrick fortresses (*qalas*) and unbaked loess architecture survive with exceptional surface preservation [@Anon2024Ultrasound]. Conversely, in the intensively cultivated alluvial valleys of the Zarafshan, Ferghana and Tashkent, continuous agricultural terracing, modern urban expansion and Soviet-era cotton monoculture have obliterated thousands of mediaeval mound sites (*tepas*), causing modern excavation inventories to under-represent rural hamlets relative to monumental citadels [@Anon2024Ultrasound; @Ibragimov2024Talk].

Third, ceramic chronologies in Central Asian archaeology frequently employ broad ceramic horizon dates spanning 100 to 200 years, making fine-grained decadal contemporaneity difficult to establish for non-monumental rural sites [@Laruelle2021Central]. Spatial kriging and non-stationary variograms mitigate this uncertainty by conditioning estimates on multi-proxy environmental indices and documented metropolitan nuclei [@Dobrynina2024Conjugacy].

Fourth, mobile pastoral nomadic demographics in the Dasht-i Qipchaq steppe leave ephemeral archaeological traces consisting primarily of kurgan burial mounds, stone markers and seasonal encampments lacking deep stratigraphy [@Laruelle2021Central; @Akhmetkul2025History]. Steppe populations are therefore calibrated through carrying capacity envelopes based on historical livestock herd ratios, seasonal pasturage areas and military tumen mobilization records rather than dense architectural counts [@Anon2024Selection; @Laruelle2021Central].
